name: Keto / ketogenic diet

lead: The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, very low-carbohydrate diet. It was developed as a medical therapy for refractory epilepsy, mainly in children, and is now popular for losing body fat and getting a leaner face and body. Some people also report it calming acne.

With little carbohydrate, the liver makes ketone bodies that replace glucose as fuel, and appetite often drops, so body fat falls. Wikipedia reports low-carbohydrate diets produce somewhat more short-term weight loss than low-fat diets, with the advantage fading over time, and a 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years. Acne effects are not covered in the sources consulted.

paras: People cut most bread, pasta, sugar and starchy foods and build meals around meat, fish, eggs, dairy, oils and low-carb vegetables, often tracking carbs to stay in ketosis. Early weight changes are partly water and show within the first weeks.

Reported effects include constipation, early fatigue, raised lipids and, rarely, ketoacidosis, with case reports documented. People with diabetes, pregnancy or medical conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician first.

angle.text: Very low carbohydrate intake lowers appetite and body fat for a leaner face and body, and some users report calmer skin. Keto is an established epilepsy therapy with mixed weight loss results; acne effects were not covered in the sources here.

lead: The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, very low-carbohydrate diet in which the liver produces ketone bodies as fuel. It was developed as a medical therapy for refractory epilepsy, mainly in children.[1] Popularly it is used for weight loss, and some in looksmaxxing communities also use it for leaning out and for acne claims.

For weight loss, Wikipedia reports that low-carbohydrate diets produce somewhat more short-term loss than low-fat diets, with the advantage fading over time, and a 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years.[2] Acne effects are not covered in the sources consulted.

paras: The term ketogenic diet was coined in 1921 by Russell Wilder at the Mayo Clinic, and Mynie Peterman formulated the classic diet in the 1920s, reporting in 1925 that 60 percent of 37 children became seizure-free.[1] The diet declined after phenytoin arrived in 1938 and revived in the 1990s.[1] Earlier low-carbohydrate regimens include William Banting's 1863 letter and Robert Atkins's 1972 book.[2]
Short- and medium-term studies show somewhat more loss than low-fat diets, around 100 kcal a day, fading over time, and calorie intake and adherence largely determine long-term results.[2]

Reported effects include constipation, low-grade acidosis, raised blood lipids, and early lethargy that usually resolves within two weeks.[1] Low-carbohydrate diets have been associated in case reports with ketoacidosis, and common effects include headache, bad breath and cramps.[2]

Trials in epilepsy found seizures reduced by more than 50 percent in about half of patients.[1] Trials of low-carbohydrate diets for weight loss are summarized above.[2] No studies found on ketogenic diets for acne in the sources consulted.

timeline.event: Wilder coins the term ketogenic diet.[1]
Peterman reports seizure freedom in 60% of 37 children.[1]
Atkins publishes Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution.[2]
